extracted.intended_audience: engineers, scientifically literate readers, and policymakers interested in comparative evaluation of natural energy sources and electric transmission; also readers of popular science on longevity
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical considerations for assessing the economic and technical viability of tidal, wind, rain, and water power and for validating claims and factors related to extreme human longevity. Includes numerical examples, safety guidance for high-voltage transmission, and documentary standards for age-authentication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tidal-energy area requirement and practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: For 100 horse-power a dock area of 162,000 square metres (about forty acres) is required; the vast costliness of dock-construction is generally prohibitory of schemes using artificial dock-basins to economize tidal energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the very large area required per unit power and high construction cost, artificial tidal basins are usually uneconomic except in a very few exceptional sites where embankments are practicable. Compare the economic value of land (forty acres) versus continuous 100 hp when judging feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of accumulators to store tidal/wind energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulating short 'harvests' of energy (e.g., from a tide-mill or windmill) for later use using accumulators such as Faure's electric accumulator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faure cell example: a 20 kg cell yields ~60 candle-hours; charging can be done in 6–12 hours with good economy; discharge can be wasteful in 2 hours or economical over 5 hours to a week or more. Evaluate storage capacity needed (e.g., number of cells) relative to expected calm periods and daily usage when judging wind/tidal lighting schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land value vs. energy-value trade-off for tidal basin projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic decision whether to use land (forty acres) as agricultural land or to construct tidal works to obtain continuous horsepower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare annual cost of producing equivalent power by steam (coal) vs. the rental/value of the land that would be required for tidal basins; local land values and rentals strongly affect the answer and may make tidal works unjustifiable in most locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability of sea-wall/estuary embankments
rubrics_metrics.description: Building a sea-wall across a natural basin or estuary to utilize tidal filling and emptying is only advantageous at very few locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cases it may be cheaper or more valuable to reclaim the basin as fertile land rather than to use it for tidal power; only rare sites justify the expense of embankments for tidal-energy schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wind-power prospects and revival conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wind currently supplies a substantial amount of energy (notably at sea), but windmills on land have declined; wind may regain importance as coal becomes scarce and expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-term fuel-price trajectories and local wind resources; wind can possibly supplant coal for some uses (e.g., lighting) if suitable dynamos and accumulators are paired with low-cost windmills or future inventions reduce windmill cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability of wind-driven lighting (dynamo + accumulator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using windmills to drive dynamos and charge Faure accumulators to provide incandescent lighting and store energy for use when wind fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate accumulator storage needed to cover typical calm durations (example: five days' storage), calculate number of accumulator cells required to match conventional gas lighting (example: 32 20-kg cells to equal four 16-candle gas burners), and compare total cost (dynamo + accumulator + windmill) to the prime cost of an equivalent steam-engine-driven system. Current windmill construction costs make many such plans uneconomic without further inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of artificial elevated tanks for rain-power on flat country
rubrics_metrics.description: To supply continuous 1 horsepower by storing rain in a tank 100 m high with 0.75 m annual rainfall requires ~3,153 square metres of tank area; prime cost and land value make such schemes prohibitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial elevated storage for rain-power on flat country is typically uneconomic; use natural hill drainage and waterfalls where possible instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural drainage and local placement for water-power
rubrics_metrics.description: For significant work by rain/water-power, water-wheels must be located where natural fall/drainage exists (hill-country or natural waterfalls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long aqueducts or underground pipes to carry water long distances are usually too expensive for power applications; town water supplies rarely have spare head energy sufficient for large-scale power without waste of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric (electro-magnetic) transmission of water-power is practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Dynamos (e.g., Gramme and Siemens) allow conversion of hydraulic potential into electric current for transmission over long distances with excellent economy, making remote utilization (e.g., Niagara to cities) feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess system-level economy using formulas for conductor dissipation and potential; high voltage is essential for economy. Practical demonstration and calculations (see Niagara example) indicate acceptable losses at distances of hundreds of miles with appropriate conductor sizing and voltage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical design parameters for long-distance high-voltage transmission (Niagara example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example recommended parameters: produce 80,000 volts difference at sending end; use a solid copper conductor 0.5 inch (1.27 cm) diameter over 300 statute miles (483 km); maintain remote end at 64,000 V by loads; expected current and losses yield ~80% delivered and ~20% dissipated as heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the example: expect ~26,250 hp taken at source, ~5,250 hp (20%) lost to heat, ~21,000 hp delivered. Wire temperature rise modest (~20°C) if hung in the open; dielectric (striking) distance for 80,000 V between flat metallic surfaces ~18 mm — insulation manageable. Cost of copper and its interest must be balanced against operating savings; if conductor loss cost is larger than interest on added copper, increase conductor cross-section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety threshold for domestic voltage
rubrics_metrics.description: Voltages above ~200 volts should not be admitted into houses, ships, or places where absolute, permanently reliable safeguards against accident cannot be guaranteed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High transmission potentials (e.g., 80,000 V) are acceptable in workshops or transmission mains with proper protections, but distribution to end-users should be at much lower, safe voltages via step-down apparatus or accumulators/systems that isolate high potential from domestic environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faure-battery-based receiving and distribution scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of large step-down dynamos at receiving stations, keep a large Faure battery (e.g., ~40,000 cells) charged from the high-voltage main and systematically rotate sets of cells (groups of ~50) into local town supply circuits while recharging others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate a methodical system of removing and placing sets of cells to maintain near-constant battery size; this can simplify distribution and reduce complexity compared to step-down dynamos, but requires planning of cell numbers, charging schedule, and handling logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary standards for authenticating extreme ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of exceptional longevity are best authenticated by extracts from baptismal registers or comparable contemporaneous official records rather than by declarations of the interested parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer primary ecclesiastical or civil records; life-assurance company records can be useful but may undercount lower-class longevity; be aware of incentives to exaggerate ages and possible calendar/time-division differences in historical sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical evaluation of ancient and historical longevity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient claims of extreme ages (patriarchs, classical centenarians) may be affected by differing calendars, legendary accounts, or local motives to claim advanced age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize contemporaneity and motive; where possible corroborate with multiple independent documents; treat aggregated census or self-reported ages with caution due to potential interest in inflating age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifestyle and hereditary factors as indicators of potential longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported common traits among centenarians include temperance (sobriety), regular habits, freedom from care, indefatigable walking/exercise, early to bed and early to rise; hereditary longevities are frequently observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing likelihood of exceptional lifespan for an individual or population, consider family history (heredity), occupation (agricultural workers more represented historically), and consistent healthy habits as positive correlates; note these are associations, not guaranteed predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological scaling rules relating maturity age to lifespan
rubrics_metrics.description: Several physiologists propose that total duration of life is proportional to the time required to reach maturity (examples: Buffon 6×, Flourens 5×, Hufeland 8×).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such proportional rules cautiously as heuristic bounds for 'ideal' lifespan estimates rather than hard maxima; different authors apply different multipliers based on comparative observations among species and presumed maturity ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of autopsy and medical evidence in assessing extraordinary longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical-autopsy findings (e.g., sound viscera in very old individuals) can support the credibility that an individual might have lived longer under unchanged conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autopsy evidence should be considered alongside documentary proof; medical condition at death may indicate whether claimed age was biologically plausible, but it cannot substitute for documentary authentication of birth/age.
